name: Agentic and Corrective RAG
question: Should the agent plan, check and retry its own retrieval?
summary: An agent plans retrieval instead of running one fixed search. It pulls structured filters out of the question, chooses the collection or tool, and checks what came back. Corrective RAG (CRAG) adds a grader that scores the retrieved passages: weak results trigger a rewritten query, a different source such as web search, or an honest “not found”. Self-querying retrieval is the filter-extraction part of this pattern.
useCases: Questions with implicit filters: dates, prices, categories, owners
Several collections or data sources to choose between
Hard questions where a first search often misses

items.detail: “laptops under ₹60k from 2024” → price and year filters
which collection, index or tool to query
a small model scores each passage: relevant, ambiguous or wrong
rewrite, switch source or abstain when grades are low
top-k, filters and a cap on retries

steps: Have the agent output a structured query plan that code validates
Grade the retrieved passages before generating
Rewrite, switch source or abstain when grades are low, with a hard cap on retries
Log every plan and grade, and compare against a fixed pipeline on your eval set
pitfalls: Adds LLM calls and latency before every answer
A wrong filter silently excludes the right results
Unbounded retry loops; always cap them
remember: Plan the query, grade the results, retry or admit defeat.
caption: The plan is plain JSON, so code can validate filters before anything runs.

comparison.needs: Implicit filters, many sources, hard questions

steps.title: Describe the plan schema
steps.text: A typed plan lists the fields the database can filter on, with ranges and allowed values. The model can only fill these fields.

steps.title: Let the model fill the plan
steps.text: The request becomes a semantic query plus structured filters: year 2024 and a price ceiling. Here the model slips and writes 60.

steps.title: Validate the plan in code
steps.text: ge=10_000 rejects a price of 60 before any search runs. The error goes back to the model, which returns 60,000.

steps.title: Run the structured search
steps.text: Filters are applied exactly by the database; only the “long battery life” part is matched by meaning.

steps.title: Check the results, retry once
steps.text: Fewer than 3 hits triggers one re-plan with feedback. The loop is capped so a bad request can't spin forever.

steps.title: Log every plan
steps.text: Store the request, the plan and the hit count. Silent wrong filters only show up when someone reads these logs or an eval set catches them.

pros: Turns implicit constraints into exact filters
Grading lets the pipeline retry or say “not found” instead of guessing
A corrective step can switch source when the first search is weak
Plans and grades are plain data you can validate, log and replay
cons: Adds LLM latency and cost to every query
A wrong but valid filter silently hides correct results
Harder to test than a fixed pipeline
Retry loops multiply cost unless capped
avoidWhen: Queries carry no structured constraints (a fixed pipeline is cheaper)
Hard latency limits well under a second leave no room for an LLM call

samples.code:
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

class SearchPlan(BaseModel):
    query: str
    max_price: int | None
    launch_year: int | None
    must_have: list[str]
    mode: Literal["hybrid", "vector", "keyword"]
    k: int = Field(le=50)

plan = client.beta.chat.completions.parse(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": "Turn the request into a search plan. Current year: 2026."},
              {"role": "user", "content": "gaming laptop under 80k with RTX, launched this year"}],
    response_format=SearchPlan,
).choices[0].message.parsed

print(plan)   # query='gaming laptop' max_price=80000 launch_year=2026 must_have=['RTX'] ...
results = search(plan)                   # your DB call, filters applied as structured fields

numericDrill.question: Turn “2 BHK flats in Pune under 60 lakh, ready to move” into a search plan.
numericDrill.answer: query: “2 BHK flat”; filters: city = Pune, bedrooms = 2, price < 6,000,000, status = ready_to_move; mode: hybrid; k: 10–20. Code checks the city against known values and the price as a number before running.

interview.question: What is self-querying retrieval?
interview.answer: An LLM turns a natural-language request into a semantic query plus structured metadata filters that the database applies exactly. It fixes requests with implicit constraints that pure vector search ignores.

interview.question: How do you make agentic retrieval safe and debuggable?
interview.answer: Constrain the plan to a typed schema, validate fields and values in code, cap retries, log every plan with its results, and compare against a fixed pipeline on an eval set.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the model write raw SQL or filters unchecked
mistakes.fix: Use a structured plan validated in code
Cap retries and fall back to a fixed pipeline

quiz.question: A buyer asks for “2 BHK flats in Pune under 60 lakh”. What max_price_inr should the plan contain?
The planner writes max_price_inr = 60 for “under 60k”. What catches it before any search runs?
options: A range check such as ge=10,000 in the schema
quiz.explanation: Validation in code rejects impossible values and sends the error back to the model.

quiz.question: Which of these should a query optimization agent decide? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: The agent plans the query. The embedding model is fixed when the index is built.

quiz.question: A request needs 2 LLM calls at about 700 ms and 2 searches at about 40 ms. How much latency does the agent add?
An investor asks for “large-cap funds with an expense ratio under 1%”. What should the plan contain?
options: The whole sentence embedded as one query
Filters category = large cap and expense_ratio < 1.0, with little left for the semantic part
BM25 over the fund names only
quiz.explanation: Both constraints are structured fields; embeddings would only nudge similarity.

quiz.question: “Laptops launched this year” comes back as year = 2024 when it is 2026. What fixes it?
options: A tighter year range in the schema
Putting today’s date in the system prompt
quiz.explanation: The model cannot know the current date. A range check passes 2024, so the date must come from the prompt.

quiz.question: Which practices make agentic retrieval safe? Select all that apply.
options: A typed plan schema validated in code
Logging every plan with its results
Letting the model write raw SQL that runs directly
quiz.explanation: Structured, validated plans with capped retries and logs are safe. Unchecked raw SQL is not.

quiz.question: An assistant must choose between HR, IT and finance knowledge bases. Which agent decision is this?
options: Source selection: routing to the right collection
quiz.explanation: Choosing which collection or tool to query is source selection.

quiz.question: An agent may try up to 3 plans, each with a 700 ms LLM call and a 40 ms search. What is the worst-case added latency?
Which agent failure is hardest to notice?
options: A valid filter with a wrong value that still returns plenty of results
quiz.explanation: Nothing fires for a plausible wrong filter. Only logs and an evaluation set reveal it.

quiz.question: On 300 labelled queries, the agent gets 252 right and the fixed pipeline 219. What are their accuracies?
quiz.explanation: 252 ÷ 300 = 0.84 and 219 ÷ 300 = 0.73, a gain of 11 percentage points.

quiz.question: Queries are purely semantic, with no filters, and the latency budget is 150 ms. What do you choose?
options: A fixed pipeline, because an LLM call would break the budget
quiz.explanation: With no structured constraints and a tight budget, planning adds cost with no benefit.

quiz.question: What belongs in the agent’s description of each collection? Select all that apply.
options: Allowed values, such as practice areas
quiz.explanation: The agent needs fields, values and contents to plan well. Vectors are useless to it.

quiz.question: Which LangChain component turns a request into a query plus metadata filters?
quiz.explanation: SelfQueryRetriever asks an LLM for a semantic query and structured filters for the vector store.

quiz.question: What does the Weaviate Query Agent do?
options: Turns natural-language questions into filtered searches across collections
quiz.explanation: It chooses collections, filters and search methods from a plain-language question, on Weaviate Cloud.

quiz.question: A plan filters department = “Cardio”, but the stored value is “Cardiology”. Which measures prevent this kind of error? Select all that apply.
options: List allowed values in the schema, for example as an enum
Validate values in code before searching
Log plans and review filters that return few results
quiz.explanation: Constrained values, validation and logs catch wrong values. A larger k cannot fix a filter that matches nothing.

quiz.question: Which self-check design is sound?
options: Re-plan once with feedback when results are too few, then fall back
Always drop every filter on retry
quiz.explanation: One capped retry with feedback recovers weak searches without runaway cost.

quiz.question: What does adding a query optimization agent cost? Select all that apply.
options: More cost when retries run, unless they are capped
A larger vector index on disk
quiz.explanation: The agent adds LLM calls. The index itself is unchanged.

quiz.question: A handler asks for “claims above INR 2 lakh”. What value should the amount filter use?
quiz.explanation: 2 lakh = 2 × 100,000 = 200,000, written 2,00,000 in Indian notation.

quiz.question: The plan asks for k = 500, but the schema allows at most 50. What should happen?
options: Validation fails, and the model is asked again or k is clamped to 50
quiz.explanation: The schema is the contract: invalid plans are rejected or corrected before any search.
